course: Fortified Corn-Soy Porridge for Malnourished Children
module_title: Sourcing and Storing Corn and Soybeans Locally

lessons.title: Where to buy quality corn and soybeans in local markets
lessons.body:
Start by visiting at least three different markets or traders in your area. In many African countries, the best quality corn and soybeans come directly from farmers or from market vendors who specialize in grains. Look for vendors who sell in bulk, not those who repackage small quantities. Ask other food processors, millers, or nutrition centers where they buy their ingredientsâthey often know the most reliable sources.

When you go to the market, inspect the grain yourself. Good corn kernels should be uniform in color, hard, and free of cracks. Avoid corn that looks dusty, has a musty smell, or shows any green or black spotsâthese are signs of mold. Soybeans should be clean, round, and free of shriveled or damaged seeds. Never buy grain that is already ground into flour; you cannot check its quality. Always buy whole grains.

Bring a small clean container and a moisture meter if you have one. A simple moisture meter costs about $20â$50 and can save you from buying wet grain that will mold. If you don't have a meter, squeeze a few kernels between your teethâgood dry corn should be hard and shatter, not soft or chewy. For soybeans, bite oneâit should be hard and dry, not rubbery. Aim for moisture content below 13% for corn and below 12% for soybeans.

Buy from farmers who have a reputation for good storage. Ask if they use hermetic bags or proper drying. Visit their storage if possible. Avoid buying from open-air piles on the ground, especially during the rainy season. If you see insects, weevils, or cobwebs, move on. A good supplier will let you take a sample home to test before you commit to a large purchase. Start with a small trial batch, test it for aflatoxin (see Lesson 2), and only then buy in bulk.

lessons.title: How to check for aflatoxin in corn and groundnuts
lessons.body:
Aflatoxin is a poison produced by mold that grows on corn and groundnuts, especially when they are dried or stored poorly. It can cause liver cancer and stunted growth in children. You cannot see, smell, or taste aflatoxin, so you must test for it. The good news is that simple, low-cost test kits are available in many African countries.

The most common test is the enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay (ELISA) kit, which costs about $1â$3 per sample. You can buy these from agricultural supply stores or from companies like Romer Labs or Neogen. To use it, grind a small sample of grain (about 100 grams) in a clean coffee grinder or mortar and pestle. Mix it with the provided solvent, shake, and let it settle. Then add a few drops to the test strip or well. After 5â10 minutes, a color change tells you if aflatoxin is present. Compare the color to the chart provided. A safe level for children's food is below 10 parts per billion (ppb); anything above 20 ppb should be rejected.

If you cannot afford test kits, you can use a black light (UV lamp) in a dark room. Aflatoxin glows a bright greenish-yellow under UV light. Spread a thin layer of ground corn or groundnuts on a clean surface and shine the light. Pick out any glowing kernels or particles. However, this method only detects high levels and is not reliable for low-level contamination. It is better than nothing, but not a substitute for a proper test.

Always test each new batch of corn or groundnuts before you use them, especially if you buy from a new supplier. Keep a record of test results. If a batch tests positive, do not use it for children's porridge. You can try to reduce aflatoxin by soaking the grain in water with 1% lime (calcium hydroxide) for 24 hours, then rinsing and dryingâbut this only reduces, not eliminates, the toxin. The safest action is to reject the batch and find a new supplier. Train your workers to recognize the signs of moldy grain and to never mix good grain with suspect grain.

lessons.title: Proper drying and storage of corn and soybeans to prevent mold
lessons.body:
Mold grows when grain is too wet. To prevent mold, you must dry corn and soybeans to a safe moisture level: below 13% for corn and below 12% for soybeans. You can test moisture with a cheap moisture meter (available for $20â$50) or by the salt method: mix a handful of grain with dry salt in a sealed jar, shake for 2 minutes, and if the salt sticks to the sides, the grain is still too wet.

Drying is best done on a clean concrete floor or on a black plastic tarp in full sun. Spread the grain in a thin layer, no more than 5 cm deep, and rake it every 30 minutes. In hot, sunny weather, corn dries in 2â3 days and soybeans in 1â2 days. Bring the grain indoors at night or cover it with a tarp to prevent dew or rain from wetting it again. Never dry grain on bare groundâit picks up dirt, moisture, and mold spores.

After drying, clean the grain by winnowing or sieving to remove broken kernels, dust, and foreign matter. Broken kernels mold faster. Then store the grain in airtight containers. The best options are hermetic storage bags (like GrainPro or PICS bags), metal silos, or plastic drums with tight-fitting lids. These exclude air and stop insects and mold. If you use jute or polypropylene sacks, stack them on wooden pallets, not directly on the floor, and keep them in a dry, well-ventilated room. Never store grain in a room that has leaks or floods.

Add a desiccant like dried neem leaves or silica gel packets to absorb moisture. Check stored grain every two weeks. Look for clumping, a musty smell, or discoloration. If you find mold, remove the affected grain immediately and dry the rest again. For long-term storage, keep the room temperature below 25Â°C and relative humidity below 65%. A simple thermometer and hygrometer cost less than $15. Proper drying and storage can keep your grain safe for 6â12 months.

lessons.title: Working with local farmers to get consistent supply
lessons.body:
To run a reliable porridge business, you need a steady supply of good-quality corn and soybeans. The best way is to work directly with local smallholder farmers. Start by visiting farmers in your area during planting season. Introduce yourself and explain that you need a consistent quantity of grain every month. Ask about their farm size, what they grow, and how they store their harvest. Look for farmers who already dry and store their grain well.

Offer a fair price and a clear contract. A simple written agreement (even handwritten) stating the quantity, quality, price, and delivery date protects both of you. For example, you might agree to buy 500 kg of corn and 200 kg of soybeans every month at a set price. Pay a small deposit (10â20%) at planting time to help the farmer buy seeds or fertilizer, and pay the rest on delivery. This builds trust and ensures the farmer prioritizes your order.

Provide training and support. Teach farmers how to dry grain to below 13% moisture, how to use hermetic storage bags, and how to avoid aflatoxin. You can organize a short workshop or share printed guides. If you can, buy a moisture meter and let farmers test their grain before selling. Farmers who learn these skills will produce better grain, and you will have less waste. Consider forming a farmer group of 5â10 farmers so you can buy in bulk and share transport costs.

Plan for the off-season. Corn and soybeans are harvested once or twice a year. To have supply all year, you need to buy enough at harvest and store it properly. Work with farmers to store a portion of their harvest for you, or rent a community warehouse. Offer a bonus for farmers who deliver clean, dry, mold-free grain. Keep records of each farmer's deliveries, quality, and payment. This helps you identify your best suppliers and plan for next season. Consistent supply means consistent production, which is key to keeping malnourished children fed.

lessons.title: Negotiating prices for bulk purchases at harvest time
lessons.body:
Harvest time is when prices are lowest, so this is the best time to buy in bulk. But you must negotiate wisely. Before you go to the market, find out the current market price. Ask other buyers, check radio announcements, or call a few farmers. Know the price per kilogram for both corn and soybeans. In many African countries, corn prices drop by 30â50% at harvest compared to the lean season. For example, if corn is $0.50/kg in the lean season, it might be $0.25â$0.35/kg at harvest.

When you negotiate, buy in large quantities. Farmers and traders give discounts for bulk. For instance, buying 1,000 kg might get you a 10% discount, while buying 5,000 kg could get you 20%. Bring cash or a mobile money transfer to pay immediatelyâmany sellers offer a lower price for cash. Always inspect the grain before agreeing on a price. If you find mold, insects, or high moisture, ask for a lower price or reject the lot. Be polite but firm. Remember that you are not just buying grain; you are building a relationship.

Consider forming a buying group with other porridge producers or nutrition centers. Pool your money and buy a full truckload (10â30 tonnes). This gives you more bargaining power and reduces transport costs per kilogram. You can also negotiate with farmers' cooperatives, which often have better quality control and can supply larger volumes. Ask for a sample before you commit. Test the sample for aflatoxin (see Lesson 2). If it passes, sign a simple contract with the price, quantity, and delivery date.

Timing is critical. The best prices are within 2â4 weeks after harvest, before traders start hoarding. If you wait too long, prices rise. Also, consider buying directly from farmers rather than through middlemenâyou save 10â20%. But if you buy from farmers, you may need to arrange transport and storage. Always keep a record of your purchases, including price, quantity, and supplier. This helps you compare prices next season and negotiate better. A good deal at harvest means affordable porridge for children all year.

lessons.title: Setting up a small storage room to keep ingredients safe
lessons.body:
A proper storage room protects your corn and soybeans from moisture, pests, and mold. You don't need a big buildingâa small room (2m x 3m) can store up to 2 tonnes of grain if organized well. Choose a room that is dry, well-ventilated, and away from kitchens or bathrooms. It should have a solid floor (concrete is best), walls without cracks, and a ceiling to keep out dust and rain. If you don't have a dedicated room, you can use a corner of a warehouse or a secure shed.

Start by cleaning the room thoroughly. Remove all old grain, dust, and cobwebs. Repair any leaks or holes. Paint the walls with whitewash (lime and water) to deter insects and make it easier to see dirt. Install shelves or pallets to keep bags off the floor. Wooden pallets are good, but plastic pallets are better because they don't absorb moisture. Stack bags at least 10 cm away from walls and 50 cm from the ceiling to allow air circulation. Never stack bags higher than 10 layers for jute or 15 layers for hermetic bags.

Control temperature and humidity. Aim for below 25Â°C and below 65% relative humidity. Use a thermometer and hygrometer (cost: $10â$20) to monitor daily. If humidity is too high, use a dehumidifier or place bowls of quicklime (calcium oxide) in corners to absorb moisture. Ventilate the room in the early morning or evening when the air is dry. Avoid opening the room during hot, humid afternoons. Install mesh screens on windows and vents to keep out insects and rodents. Set traps for rats and mice.

Store different grains separately. Keep corn in one section and soybeans in another to prevent cross-contamination and make inventory easier. Use hermetic bags or airtight drums for long-term storage. Label each bag with the date, supplier, and moisture level. Rotate stockâuse the oldest grain first. Inspect the room weekly for signs of mold, insects, or water damage. Keep a broom, dustpan, and flashlight handy. A well-maintained storage room can keep your ingredients safe for 6â12 months, ensuring you always have quality grain for your porridge.

quiz.q: What is the best place to buy quality corn and soybeans?
options: A) Open-air piles on the ground
B) Directly from farmers or specialized grain vendors
C) Supermarkets that sell small packets
D) Roadside stalls that repackage grain
quiz.explanation: Buying directly from farmers or specialized vendors gives you better quality control and often lower prices.

quiz.q: Which of these is a sign of poor-quality corn?
options: A) Uniform color and hard kernels
B) Musty smell and green spots
quiz.explanation: Musty smell and green spots indicate mold and possible aflatoxin contamination.

quiz.q: What is the safe moisture content for storing corn?
quiz.explanation: Corn should be dried to below 13% moisture to prevent mold growth.

quiz.q: How can you test grain moisture without a meter?
options: A) Squeeze a kernel between your teeth
quiz.explanation: Biting a kernel is a simple field test: dry corn shatters, wet corn is soft.

quiz.q: What is aflatoxin?
options: B) A poison produced by mold
quiz.explanation: Aflatoxin is a toxic substance produced by molds that grow on poorly stored grains.

quiz.q: Which test kit is commonly used for aflatoxin?
quiz.explanation: ELISA kits are low-cost and widely used for detecting aflatoxin in grains.

quiz.q: What is the safe level of aflatoxin for children's food?
quiz.explanation: For children, aflatoxin should be below 10 parts per billion (ppb).

quiz.q: What does aflatoxin look like under UV light?
quiz.explanation: Aflatoxin fluoresces a bright greenish-yellow under UV light.

quiz.q: How can you reduce aflatoxin in contaminated grain?
quiz.explanation: Soaking in 1% lime (calcium hydroxide) solution can reduce aflatoxin levels, though it does not eliminate them completely.

quiz.q: What is the best surface for drying grain?
options: B) Concrete floor or black plastic tarp
quiz.explanation: Concrete or black plastic tarps reflect heat and keep grain clean and dry.

quiz.q: How often should you rake grain while drying?
quiz.explanation: Raking every 30 minutes speeds drying and prevents mold.

quiz.q: Which storage method is best for preventing mold and insects?
options: A) Jute sacks on the floor
B) Hermetic bags or airtight drums
D) Polypropylene sacks in a corner
quiz.explanation: Hermetic bags and airtight drums exclude air and pests, preventing mold and insect damage.

quiz.q: How often should you inspect stored grain?
quiz.explanation: Regular inspection every two weeks helps catch mold or pests early.

quiz.q: What is a good way to build trust with local farmers?
options: B) Offer a fair price and a written contract
quiz.explanation: A fair price and clear contract build long-term relationships and consistent supply.

quiz.q: Why is it good to pay a deposit to farmers at planting time?
options: A) It helps them buy inputs and prioritizes your order
C) It is required by law
D) It ensures they plant soybeans
quiz.explanation: A deposit helps farmers purchase seeds and fertilizer, and encourages them to sell to you.

quiz.q: What is a benefit of forming a farmer group?
options: A) You can buy in bulk and share transport
quiz.explanation: Farmer groups allow bulk buying, which reduces costs and improves logistics.

quiz.q: When are corn and soybean prices usually lowest?
quiz.explanation: Prices drop at harvest when supply is abundant.

quiz.q: What is a good strategy for negotiating bulk purchases?
options: B) Buy large quantities and ask for a discount
quiz.explanation: Bulk buying gives you bargaining power for discounts.

quiz.q: Why is it important to test a sample before buying in bulk?
options: A) To check for aflatoxin and quality
quiz.explanation: Testing ensures the grain is safe and meets quality standards before you commit.

quiz.q: What is a buying group?
options: B) A group of buyers pooling money to buy in bulk
D) A type of storage bag
quiz.explanation: A buying group combines resources to buy larger quantities at lower prices.

quiz.q: What is the ideal relative humidity for a storage room?
quiz.explanation: Keeping humidity below 65% prevents mold growth.

quiz.q: What is a good material for pallets in a storage room?
quiz.explanation: Plastic pallets do not absorb moisture and are easy to clean.

quiz.q: How far should bags be stacked from walls?
quiz.explanation: Leaving 10 cm allows air circulation and prevents moisture buildup.

quiz.q: What is a sign of mold in stored grain?
quiz.explanation: Clumping and musty smell indicate mold growth.

quiz.q: What is the best way to control insects in a storage room?
options: A) Use mesh screens and traps
D) Store grain on the floor
quiz.explanation: Mesh screens and traps keep insects and rodents out without chemicals.

quiz.q: Why should you label stored bags?
options: A) To track date, supplier, and moisture
B) To make them look nice
quiz.explanation: Labels help with inventory and ensure you use older stock first.

quiz.q: What is the first step in setting up a storage room?
options: A) Clean and repair the room
quiz.explanation: A clean, repaired room prevents contamination and pest entry.

quiz.q: How can you reduce moisture in a storage room?
options: A) Use quicklime or a dehumidifier
quiz.explanation: Quicklime or dehumidifiers absorb excess moisture from the air.

quiz.q: What is the maximum stack height for jute bags?
quiz.explanation: Stacking more than 10 layers can crush the bottom bags and cause spoilage.

quiz.q: Why is it important to rotate stock?
options: A) To use older grain first and prevent spoilage
quiz.explanation: Rotating stock ensures you use older grain before it goes bad.
